title: Why Hot Grease Hardens Inside Kitchen Traps
description: When hot liquid fats and cooking oils are washed down a kitchen sink, they appear to drain easily while warm. However, as wastewater travels down into the undersink P-trap, it quickly cools to match the temperature of the surrounding pipe walls and standing water seal. This rapid thermal drop causes fats, oils, and grease (FOG) to solidify against the interior pipe surfaces. Over time, this sticky layer catches food scraps and steadily narrows the pipe diameter, leading to stubborn clogs. To protect your drainage system, scrape heavy fats into solid waste or wipe greasy pans before washing. What method do you use to keep grease out of your drains?

visual_story: The viewer immediately notices a realistic cutaway section of an under-sink P-trap. Instead of a vague artistic pipe, the visual clearly highlights the internal cross-section of the trap bend. The focal point is the thick, hardened grease coating clinging to the inside surface of the pipe wall below the water line. This visually demonstrates the physical cause of kitchen drain restriction—showing that liquid grease turns into a solid restriction once it enters cold underground or under-sink drainage piping.

on_image_text.hook: Hot grease doesn't stay liquid in your drain.
on_image_text.explanation: As warm liquid fats hit cold pipe walls and standing water, they rapidly cool and congeal into solid buildup.
on_image_text.callout: P-Trap FOG (Fats, Oils, Grease) Buildup Zone
on_image_text.takeaway: Scrape fats into the trash or wipe pans with paper towels prior to washing.
